questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the siting of a monument decides
questions.learningObjective: State what the position of a monument primarily determines
questions.stem: An architect's brief asks where a civic monument should stand. What does the siting of a monument primarily decide?

options.text: The terms on which the monument is seen and understood, since meaning depends on its relation to the city
The total cost of the project, since every location carries a different price for foundations and paving
options.misconception: reduces siting to a question of foundation cost

options.text: The number of visitors, since the most accessible position will always attract the largest crowd
options.misconception: treats access and footfall as the whole of siting

options.text: The material the monument is made from, since the local stone is chosen to suit the site
options.misconception: assumes the site alone dictates the material

questions.explanation: Siting fixes the monument relationships to streets, buildings and crowds, and those determine how the work is read. Cost, footfall and material are inputs, not what the position settles.
questions.hint: Ask what the position puts the monument in relation to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial argument of a memorial garden
questions.learningObjective: Compare the spatial arguments of a formal and an informal garden
questions.stem: A brief compares two memorial garden layouts: Scheme A places a long reflecting pool at the centre of a straight axis, and Scheme B sets a single stone among irregular planting with no axis at all. What contrast is being drawn?

options.text: That the formal scheme costs more to build and the informal one is therefore the better value
options.misconception: reduces the comparison to build cost

options.text: That a formal axis directs a procession, while an informal setting offers encounter without direction
That the reflecting pool hides the names while the single stone exposes them to view
options.misconception: reads the layouts as devices for concealing names

options.text: That the irregular planting is harder to maintain and so will lose fewer visitors over time
options.misconception: confuses maintenance burden with visitor numbers

questions.explanation: A straight axis choreographs a route, while irregular planting gives an encounter without prescribed direction. The contrast is about the movement each layout asks of the visitor.
questions.hint: Ask how each layout asks the visitor to move.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The narrative a war memorial selects
questions.learningObjective: Explain how different memorials select different accounts of one history
questions.stem: A heritage committee asks why memorials to the same conflict use very different material and form. Explain what selection each one performs.

answer.exemplar: Each memorial chooses a different aspect of the same history and makes that choice in its form, its material and its setting. One design concentrates on sacrifice and shows a solitary figure against a wall of names, while another emphasises the obligation of the living and gives an open lawn and a bench instead. Both are honest about the deaths they record, and both remain partial accounts of the same history rather than complete ones.

questions.explanation: Each memorial foregrounds one aspect of the shared history and embodies that choice in form and material, so the works differ in emphasis rather than accuracy. Both remain partial accounts.
questions.hint: Ask what each design puts in the foreground.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit a cast sets on reproduction
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the detail a cast cannot reproduce from its model
questions.stem: A foundry record shows that its casts hold undercut detail down to 0.2 millimetres, while the original carving carries 0.35 millimetres of undercutting. How many millimetres of undercutting does the cast fail to reproduce?
questions.explanation: The cast cannot hold undercutting finer than 0.2 millimetres, so it loses 0.35 minus 0.2, which is 0.15 millimetres. A cast therefore sets a floor on fineness that carving itself is not bound by.
questions.hint: Subtract the reproducible detail from the original.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a photographic negative documents
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a negative records about a scene

stimulus.body: A conservator examining a photographic negative from a lost survey notes that the buildings in the image appear pale while the sky and shadows register dark. A print made from the negative shows the buildings dark against a pale sky.

questions.stem: Given the archive note, what does the negative document about the original scene?

options.text: The colours of the original view, since the plate keeps a separate colour record
options.misconception: assumes the plate preserves original colour values

options.text: The finished positive print, since the negative is an intermediate copy of the paper print
options.misconception: treats the negative as a copy of the print

options.text: The arrangement of light and shade in the scene, since the plate records brightness in reverse for printing
The camera's chosen exposure, since the plate stores the photographer's intent rather than the light
options.misconception: confuses the plate with the photographer's intention

questions.explanation: A negative records light as density in reverse, so bright sky becomes dark and shadowed wall pale, and the print reverses that. It documents tone, not colour or the photographer's intent.
questions.hint: Ask how brightness is inverted on the plate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The direction of an intaglio image
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an intaglio impression prints in reverse
questions.stem: Stage one: a printmaker etches lettering into a copper plate and prints it on damp paper. Stage two: the printed lettering reads backwards to the viewer. What is the correct account of this result?

options.text: The reversal is normal for this process, and it is corrected by printing a second sheet from the same plate
options.misconception: claims a second impression corrects the reversal

options.text: The plate was cut in reverse by mistake, so recutting the lettering the other way would correct the print
options.misconception: blames the engraving rather than the transfer

options.text: The lettering reads backwards because the press pushes the sheet into the plate, printing it face down
options.misconception: gives the reversal a cause it does not have

options.text: The image is reversed by the printing itself, since the sheet pressed face down takes the ink in mirror image

questions.explanation: Intaglio prints in mirror image because the sheet is pressed into inked recesses and lifts the ink facing the other way, so reversal happens at the press, not in the cutting. A second pull repeats it.
questions.hint: Ask how the sheet meets the plate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The characteristic line of relief printing
questions.learningObjective: Identify the line quality produced by a relief block
questions.stem: A brief specifies an illustration printed from a block in which the areas to print stand up and the surrounding areas are cut away. What line quality does this produce?

options.text: A line that varies in depth with the pressure of the press, since the ink is forced into the cut recesses
options.misconception: describes intaglio behaviour instead of relief

options.text: A bold and even line of uniform thickness, since the cut areas take no ink and the raised edges define it
A soft and broken edge, since the ink spreads into the damp paper from the carved recesses
options.misconception: confuses the damp paper effect of intaglio with relief

options.text: A line that reverses the direction of the original drawing, since the block prints in reverse
options.misconception: treats reversal as the defining mark of relief

questions.explanation: Only the raised surface carries ink in relief printing, giving a clear edge and consistent thickness. Ink is neither pressed into recesses nor allowed to bleed, so the broken line belongs to intaglio.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the block carry the ink.

questions.stem: A survey records how long visitors stand at four sites for the same statue. Results: 90 seconds in a square, 40 in a market, 25 beside a car park, and 180 in a quiet garden. What does this suggest about siting?

options.text: That the statue is more successful in quiet places, because noise always reduces appreciation
options.misconception: generalises from one comparison to a rule

options.text: That the garden site is the only one worth keeping, since the others attracted too few visitors
options.misconception: judges sites by attention time alone

options.text: That the surroundings govern how the work is received, so attention depends on what the monument stands among
That the timings measure the weather at each site, since a longer stay suggests colder conditions
options.misconception: reads the timings as environmental rather than spatial

questions.explanation: The same work held attention for very different lengths of time in different settings, so surroundings govern how it is received. One good site does not make the others failures.
questions.hint: Ask what was held constant across the four sites.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial argument of a memorial garden
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a garden argues through a route rather than a view
questions.stem: A landscape brief asks why a memorial garden should be designed as a route rather than as a single view. Explain the argument such a route makes.

answer.exemplar: A route moves the visitor through a sequence, and each stage can add one element of the argument while the previous element recedes. The garden can begin with an open lawn that offers rest, then narrow to a walled walk where the names are read at close range, and end at a stone placed against a horizon that leaves the meaning open. Seen all at once from a single point the same elements would collapse into one image and lose the ordering that gives each its place.

questions.explanation: A route builds its argument in sequence, so each element means more because of what precedes and follows. A single view collapses that order into one image and loses the progression.
questions.hint: Ask what sequencing adds to the elements.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the panels needed to record a list of names
questions.stem: A memorial lists the names of 480 fallen and also records 2,100 who served. If the panel can carry 60 names, how many panels are needed to list all the fallen?
questions.explanation: Each panel carries 60 names, so 480 divided by 60 gives exactly 8 panels. The 2,100 who served shows what the naming leaves out, since the panels record the dead alone.
questions.hint: Divide the number of names by the names per panel.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit a cast sets on reproduction
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a cast can and cannot carry from its model

stimulus.body: A studio memo records a bronze edition produced from a single carved plaster model. The carver's fingerprint ridges appear on the surface of the finished bronze, and the note adds that the model was destroyed after casting, leaving no record of the original.

questions.stem: Given the studio memo, what limitation does the cast place on the reproduction?

options.text: It is a loose interpretation, because the mould loses most of the model's detail in the casting
options.misconception: overstates the loss of detail in casting

options.text: It improves on the model, since metal records the surface more finely than plaster ever does
options.misconception: claims the cast surpasses the model it copies

options.text: It is identical in every respect, since the metal replaces the model exactly as it was
options.misconception: assumes exact identity between cast and model

options.text: It can capture what the model happened to contain, but it cannot supply anything the model never recorded

questions.explanation: A cast transfers what is present in the model, including flaws and fingerprints, and adds nothing never modelled. It does not lose detail indiscriminately, so the bronze is neither better nor vaguer.
questions.hint: Ask what the mould could possibly add.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a photographic negative documents
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a photographic negative records
questions.stem: Stage two: a photographer exposes a plate of a building with a bright sky. Stage one: the print made from that plate shows a dark sky and a pale building. What has the negative recorded?

options.text: The finished print exactly as it will be seen, since the plate is a one step copy of the image
options.misconception: treats the negative as a finished copy

options.text: The reversed tonal arrangement of the scene, since the plate fixed the brightness of each part in negative
The original colours of the scene, since the plate preserves the colour of every surface
options.misconception: assumes colour is recorded on the plate

options.text: The outline of the building only, since tone is a property of the print and not of the plate
options.misconception: denies that the plate holds tone

questions.explanation: The plate fixes brightness in negative, so bright sky registers as density and the pale building as transparency, and the print reverses it. The negative holds tone, not colour.
questions.hint: Ask how brightness behaves in a negative.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The direction of an intaglio image
questions.learningObjective: State the relationship between an intaglio print and its plate
questions.stem: A print room asks how the image in an intaglio print relates to the image on the plate that made it. What is the relationship?

options.text: The printed image cannot be compared with the plate at all, since intaglio prints are made from photographs
options.misconception: mistakes intaglio for photographic printing

options.text: The printed image matches the plate image, because the ink is applied to the flat surface around the lines
options.misconception: assumes ink sits on the flat surface

options.text: The printed image is the reverse of the plate image, because the sheet takes ink from the recessed lines
The printed image is identical to the plate image, because the sheet records whatever lies in the recesses
options.misconception: denies the reversal that contact transfer causes

questions.explanation: Intaglio prints in reverse because the sheet is pressed into inked recesses and lifts the ink the other way. That reversal is one of two, since the plate was already inverse to the drawing.
questions.hint: Ask how the sheet meets the plate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The characteristic line of relief printing
questions.learningObjective: Predict the printed line produced by different cuts
questions.stem: A print room compares two proofs: one pulled from a woodblock whose carved lines are narrow and deep, and one from a block with broad shallow cuts. What difference in the printed line follows?

options.text: The broad shallow cuts print more faintly, because shallower cuts hold less ink than deep ones
options.misconception: reverses which cut holds more ink

options.text: The narrow deep cuts print as heavier marks, since the press drives more ink into the deeper grooves
options.misconception: confuses depth with ink coverage

options.text: Both proofs are identical, since the ink is applied to the whole block before the paper is pressed
options.misconception: assumes uniform inking erases line difference

options.text: The narrow deep cuts print as finer and sharper lines, while broad shallow cuts print as heavier flatter bands

questions.explanation: In relief printing ink sits on the raised surface, so the raised band's width sets the printed line: fine ridges give fine lines, wide ones broad bands. Cut depth affects the edge, not the ink.
questions.hint: Ask what carries the ink in a relief block.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the siting of a monument decides
questions.learningObjective: Explain why relocating a monument changes its reading
questions.stem: A civic trust asks why a monument moved from a square to a park is generally understood differently. Explain what the move changes.

answer.exemplar: A monument's meaning is produced by relationships, and a square supplies a dense set of them: crowds, commercial frontage, traffic, and the other public buildings that tell the visitor what kind of place this is. A park supplies a quieter and more spacious set, with land and sky around it rather than facades. Moving the monument does not alter the object at all, but it hands the work a different set of companions and a different kind of attention.

questions.explanation: Siting supplies the relationships that give a monument its meaning, so moving it changes how it is read even though the object is untouched. The attention a square prompts differs from a park's.
questions.hint: Ask what a square supplies that a park does not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The narrative a war memorial selects
questions.learningObjective: Identify the narrative selected by a memorial with an empty chair

stimulus.body: Two memorials stand in the same town. The first shows a standing soldier figure with the names of the fallen carved on a wall behind him. The second is an empty chair beside a hedge with no names at all. A local history group records that the second was erected by the families of those who died in the town's own air raid.

questions.stem: Given the collection note, what narrative does the second memorial select?

options.text: The individual names of the fallen, which are engraved on a separate wall not mentioned in the note
options.misconception: invents a wall of names the note does not record

options.text: The absence of the dead and the presence of daily ordinary life, which the empty chair makes the subject
The military victory of the war, which the chair position commemorates through the town's parade
options.misconception: reads the chair as a reference to military celebration

options.text: The bravery of the soldiers, which is represented by the hedge standing as a line of defences
options.misconception: reads the hedge as a symbol of military defence

questions.explanation: The empty chair offers the place of someone absent, so the work selects grief and ordinary life rather than the military record. By leaving out names and figures it argues through absence.
questions.hint: Ask what the empty chair stands in for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit a cast sets on reproduction
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cast is described as a record rather than a new object
questions.stem: An architect's brief asks why a cast of a carved panel is sometimes described as a record of an object rather than a new object. Explain what the cast preserves and what it cannot be.

answer.exemplar: A cast fixes one particular state of a carved panel at one particular moment, including the tool marks, the wear and the small accidents that the making left in the surface. In that sense it is a document. But the cast is not the panel: it has no grain, no weathering history and no continued life, and it fixes the carving in a state that was only ever one stage in a longer sequence of alteration. It can therefore preserve evidence of the panel without being the panel, and it can outlive it without replacing it.

questions.explanation: A cast captures one moment of a surface, with its marks intact, making it documentary evidence. It cannot carry the material history or keep changing, so it records rather than duplicates.
questions.hint: Ask what the cast holds still.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a photographic negative documents
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the tonal range lost between a plate and its print
questions.stem: A photographic plate records a building with 240 tones from deepest shadow to brightest sky. A print made from it shows only 60 distinct tones. What fraction of the recorded tonal range survives into the print?
questions.explanation: The print carries 60 of the 240 tones on the plate, and 60 over 240 gives one quarter, so a quarter of the range survives. The print is a compressed interpretation rather than a full copy.
questions.hint: Divide the printed tones by the recorded tones.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The direction of an intaglio image
questions.learningObjective: Explain why repeated pulls from a plate share one direction
questions.stem: Stage one: an etching is printed and the resulting image is the mirror image of the plate. Stage two: the printmaker makes a second impression from the same plate and prints it in the same way. What is the relationship between the two impressions?

options.text: They are identical and unmirrored, since only the first impression picks up ink from the recesses
options.misconception: claims the ink reaches the paper only once

options.text: The second impression is the right way round, since the plate is worn smoother and prints more accurately
options.misconception: believes wear corrects the reversal

options.text: They carry the same reversal, since each pull takes the ink out of the recesses in the same mirror orientation
The second is reversed twice and so reads correctly, because a second pull flips the plate automatically
options.misconception: invents an automatic flipping between pulls

questions.explanation: Each pull works on the same inked recesses and transfers the image in the same mirror orientation, so the second repeats the first reversal exactly. Nothing about wear or repetition flips the sheet.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the plate between the pulls.

questions.topic: The characteristic line of relief printing
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a printed line from a drawn line
questions.stem: A print room asks which feature distinguishes a line printed in relief from a line drawn in ink. What is the correct answer?

options.text: The printed line is drawn rather than cut, so it reverses the direction of the draught in every case
options.misconception: mixes the print line with a reversal of the drawing

options.text: The printed line is smoother, because the ink lies on the raised surface and covers the tool marks entirely
options.misconception: assumes relief printing hides all evidence of the tool

options.text: The printed line is identical in every case, since the cutter has no effect on the width of the line
options.misconception: denies the cutter any influence on the line

options.text: The printed line records the edge of a cut surface, so its weight comes from the tool rather than the draught

questions.explanation: A relief line is the edge of cut material, so its weight and texture record how the tool was used, which a drawn line never shows. Its character comes from the block and the blade.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial argument of a memorial garden
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a sequence of spaces does that a viewpoint cannot
questions.stem: A landscape architect defends a plan in which the visitor passes through four spaces before reaching the central stone. Explain what that sequence does that a single viewpoint cannot.

answer.exemplar: A sequence of spaces gives the visitor time to be prepared before the object of the visit is reached, and each space can carry one part of the argument while the earlier ones recede behind. A single viewpoint collapses all of it into one image, and an image is held all at once rather than taken in over time. What the sequence produces is therefore a reading that unfolds, in which the final element means something different because of the spaces that come before it.

questions.explanation: A sequence lets each space prepare the visitor for what follows, so the final element is read differently than it would be alone. A single viewpoint collapses the argument into one image.
questions.hint: Ask what the earlier spaces contribute.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit a cast sets on reproduction
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cast cannot record later changes to its model

stimulus.body: A condition note records that a bronze cast taken from a plaster model in 1931 carries the grain of the plaster mould on its surface, together with a shrinkage crack that matches one visible in the model at the time of casting. The model itself was later repaired and the crack no longer appears on it.

questions.stem: Given the condition note, what limitation on reproduction does the cast reveal?

options.text: The cast proves the crack was manufactured after the original was repaired
options.misconception: reverses the sequence of casting and repair

options.text: The cast is the more faithful version, since it preserves the original condition while the model was altered
options.misconception: treats the cast as the truer object

options.text: The cast fixes one moment of the model's condition, so it cannot record later repairs or continuing change
The cast can be updated to match the repaired model, since bronze can be recast at any time
options.misconception: assumes a cast can simply be recast to match

questions.explanation: The cast is evidence of the model's condition when the mould was taken, so it cannot report the later repair. A copy of a copy records a moment, not a version that updates itself.

options.misconception: gets the source of the reversal in the wrong place

options.misconception: denies the directional character of the image

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The characteristic line of relief printing
questions.learningObjective: Explain an irregular edge appearing in a relief proof
questions.stem: A proof from a relief block shows one line that is crisp and even and another that is fuzzy and irregular. The block was cut by hand in both cases. What explains the difference?

options.text: That the fuzzy line was printed from a worn block, since repeated use rounds every edge
options.misconception: attributes irregularity to wear on the block

options.text: That the crisp line was inked more heavily, since the two lines were rolled at different pressures

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The characteristic line of relief printing
questions.learningObjective: Compare the lines produced by woodcut and engraving
questions.stem: An editor compares the woodcut used for a broadsheet with the fine engraving used for an illustration in the same paper. Explain what gives each print its characteristic line.

answer.exemplar: The line belongs to the tool and the material it cuts, and each pair produces its own consequence. A woodcut is carved with knives and gouges into a block that splinters along the grain, so its lines swell, break and carry the roughness of the wood. An engraving is cut with a burin into metal that parts cleanly, so the line stays thin, even and disciplined at any scale the burin can reach. Neither print is the better one; they are different instruments.

questions.explanation: In relief the mark belongs to the cut, so the tool's shape and the material's resistance set the line. A woodcut breaks and swells in the grain, while an engraving holds a fine even line in metal.
questions.hint: Ask what actually makes the mark in a relief block.

answer.exemplar: In an intaglio print the lettering runs backwards, and the reason is mechanical: the sheet is pressed face down onto the inked plate and lifts the image out in mirror image, so anything the artist drew the right way round on the plate arrives on the sheet the wrong way round. The reversal is proof that the print came from an incised plate and was transferred by contact, and it is the reason the plate has to be cut backwards in the first place.

answer.exemplar: A negative is a technical record, and it is not an image in the ordinary sense until light is passed through it or it is printed: it is a patterned plate in which the densities correspond to the brightnesses that fell on it. questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The characteristic line of relief printing
questions.learningObjective: Predict printed line weight from the raised band width
questions.stem: A print room measures proofs from two blocks. Block P has raised lines averaging 3 millimetres wide; Block Q has raised bands averaging 9 millimetres. What difference in the printed result follows directly?

options.text: The lines print at the same weight, because the ink spreads out after the paper is lifted
options.misconception: assumes ink spreads to equalise them

options.text: The lines from Block P print three times heavier, since narrow bands hold more ink under the press
options.misconception: reverses the relation between band width and weight

options.text: The lines from Block P print at about a third the weight of those from Block Q, since the band carries the ink
Only Block Q can be printed, since narrow raised bands cannot take enough ink to mark the sheet
options.misconception: claims narrow bands cannot hold ink

questions.explanation: The printed line is as wide as the raised band carrying the ink, so a 3 millimetre band prints about a third of the weight of a 9 millimetre band. Ink does not spread to equalise them.
questions.hint: Ask what determines the width of the printed line.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the siting of a monument decides
questions.learningObjective: Explain how siting carries political weight
questions.stem: A committee asks why a monument's position in a city can be politically charged. Explain how location carries political weight.

answer.exemplar: Location is a claim about priorities, because a monument that stands in the newest and wealthiest part of a city announces that this part of the city is where the city's history belongs. Move the same statue to a district that was left out of that history, and the object is no longer the same thing at all, though the stone is identical. The council's choice of site therefore does the work of deciding which parts of the past the city chooses to celebrate and which it leaves to other ground.

questions.explanation: A site claims priorities, since placing a monument in one part of a city rather than another says which part its story belongs to. The stone may be identical while the political weight differs.
questions.hint: Ask what the choice of district asserts.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The spatial argument of a memorial garden
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the hedging needed along a memorial garden edge
questions.stem: A memorial garden's main walk has 12 stations and an outer path of 20. If the site is edged with a hedge of 64 metres and each hedge section covers 4 metres, how many sections are needed?
questions.explanation: The hedge needs 64 divided by 4, which is 16 sections. The station and path counts are part of the brief but do not enter this calculation, since the hedging follows the length of the edge.
questions.hint: Divide the hedge length by the length of a section.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The narrative a war memorial selects
questions.learningObjective: Interpret differing visitor readings of one memorial garden

stimulus.body: A visitor note records the reactions of a group at a war memorial garden. One visitor wrote that the walk brought the number of the dead home more clearly than any list of names had done, while another wrote that the quotations on the walls had told the story better than the planting. A guide notes that both reactions were recorded on the same day.

questions.stem: Given the visitor note, what does the disagreement between the two visitors show?

options.text: That the planting is a failure, since it fails to communicate the number of the dead to every visitor
options.misconception: treats varied responses as a failure of the planting

options.text: That one of the two visitors is mistaken about the site, since only one reading can be correct
options.misconception: assumes only one reading can be right

options.text: That the quotations are the stronger element, since named evidence always outweighs atmosphere
options.misconception: ranks one element as definitively better

options.text: That different elements of the same site carry the argument, so visitors can read one and miss another

questions.explanation: The two visitors registered different elements of the same site, showing that a memorial works through several devices at once. Visitors take different messages from it, and neither need be wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what each visitor responded to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limit a cast sets on reproduction
questions.learningObjective: State what a first cast of an unreproduced panel can claim
questions.stem: Stage one: a brief commissions a cast of a carved relief panel that has never been reproduced. Stage two: the casting succeeds and the bronze copy is installed in a public place. What claim can the copy properly make?

options.text: That it is the original work, since the model and the copy are indistinguishable to the public
options.misconception: equates the copy with the original

options.text: That it faithfully reproduces the panel form and surface, made in another material and dated after it
That it improves on the panel, because the bronze captures more of the design than the stone did
options.misconception: claims the copy surpasses the original

options.text: That it proves the panel was not carved, since a cast could only be taken from a mould
options.misconception: claims the cast disproves the carving

questions.explanation: A cast records the form and surface of the model accurately and is dated after it, so it stands as a reproduction and a document. It is not the original, and it says nothing about the making.
questions.hint: Ask what the copy can and cannot claim.
